This might be the company name or\\n   notes about the setup.\\n8. Determine which protocol you want to use for the output.\\n9. For **Port**, choose the port that\\n      you want to use when the content is distributed to this\\n      output. For more information about ports, see Output destinations.\\n\\n      **Note:**\\n\\n      The RIST protocol requires one additional port for\\n      error correction. To accommodate this requirement,\\n      AWS Elemental MediaConnect reserves the port that is +1 from\\n      the port that you specify. For example, if you\\n      specify port 4000 for the output, the service\\n      assigns ports 4000 and 4001.\\n   4. For **Smoothing latency**, specify\\n      the additional delay that you want to use with output\\n      smoothing. We recommend that you specify a value of 0 ms\\n      to disable smoothing. {"id": "50f609f1-d395-4c7d-9561-b8f45b4dac57", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_gPMdyrQTj5QZFr2ba7Ck5z", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"How do I troubleshoot network performance issues in Amazon VPC?\",\"context\":\"### Follow troubleshooting best practices\\n\\nWhen you're troubleshooting, use the following best practices:\\n\\n* Get the start and end time of the latency that you observed.\\n* Determine whether the latency issue is constant or intermittent.\\n* Determine whether changes occurred before the latency issue.\\n* Get the full network path where the latency occurs.\\n* Identify the protocols and ports in use between the source and destination networks.\\n* Activate [VPC Flow Logs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/flow-logs.html).\\n* Compare current latency to your baseline network performance.\\n* Document the actions that you take and the changes that you make\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/vpc-troubleshoot-network-performance\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"aws-media-services\",\"skill_description\":\"Designs, deploys, reviews, evaluates, audits, and troubleshoots video streaming workflows across AWS media services (MediaConnect, MediaLive, MediaConvert, MediaPackage v2, MediaTailor, CloudFront). Includes per-service validation rules, cross-service workflow patterns for live streaming, linear channels, VOD pipelines, and live-to-VOD, service-specific troubleshooting, best practices assessment, cost optimization, encoder settings, DRM, SCTE-35 ad insertion, epoch locking, and CDN cache configuration.\\n\\nServices: mediaconnect, medialive, mediaconvert, mediapackage, mediatailor, cloudfront\\nTasks: review, deploy, troubleshoot, audit, optimize\\nPersona: video-engineer, solutions-architect\\nWorkload: live-streaming, vod, linear-channel\",\"skill_name\":\"aws-media-services\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"How can I reduce the latency of HLS delivery in MediaLive?\",\"context\":\"Resolution\\n----------\\n\\nMany factors can cause delays in HLS delivery, such as encoding and decoding, network conditions, and player buffers. For more information about how to measure latency and optimize your configuration, see [How to compete with broadcast latency using current adaptive bitrate technologies](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/media/how-to-compete-with-broadcast-latency-using-current-adaptive-bitrate-technologies-part-1/).\\n\\nTo reduce latency, you can shorten the segment length of the HLS group.\\n\\n**Note:** When you shorten the segment length, your video quality might be affected and player-buffering events might increase. If you use the Low-Latency HLS (LL-HLS) workflow, then your video quality isn't affected when you shorten the segment length.\\n\\nTo shorten the segment length of the HLS group, complete the following steps:\\n\\n1. Open the [MediaLive console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/medialive/).\\n2. In the navigation pane, choose **Channels**, and then select the channel that you want to modify.\\n3. Choose **Actions**, and then choose **Edit**.\\n4. Choose the HLS output group that you want to modify.\\n5. Choose **Manifest and Segments**.\\n6. For **Segment Length**, change the value to **1**.\\n7. Choose an output in the HLS group.\\n8. Choose **GOP Structure**.\\n9. For **GOP Size Units**, select **SECONDS**.\\n10. For **GOP Size**, enter **1** to match the segment length of 1 second.\\n11. Repeat steps 7 through 10 to update every output in the HLS group.\\n12. Choose **Update Channel**.\\n\\nTo reduce latency, send your HLS output group to one the following destinations:\\n\\n* [Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/medialive/latest/ug/origin-server-hls-s3.html)\\n* [AWS Elemental MediaStore](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/medialive/latest/ug/origin-server-ems.html)\\n* [AWS Elemental MediaPackage v2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/medialive/latest/ug/origin-server-hls-empv2.html)\\n\\nRelated information\\n-------------------\\n\\n[Turning on Low-Latency HTTP live streaming (HLS)](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/http-live-streaming/enabling-low-latency-http-live-streaming-hls) on the Apple Developer website\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/medialive-reduce-latency-hls-delivery\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search AWS docs for MediaConnect SRT best practices and troubleshooting guide", "parent_id": "f1545fee-14b0-4ca3-8bda-0234c2115b8d"}

{"id": "d5ca3f10-4f5b-4398-851f-525190a6fc4b", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_ZYzM8qR6wCp5dPKiRlvcAe", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"How do I read and troubleshoot my traceroute to resolve AWS Direct Connect issues?\",\"context\":\"### Troubleshoot your traceroute\\n\\nHigh latency occurs when packets take too long to reach their destination. Hops with high RTTs cause high latency. If RTTs are consistently high across multiple traceroutes, then this indicates issues with your router or network.\\n\\nTo troubleshoot this issue, complete the following steps:\\n\\n1.\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0Open a command prompt or terminal window on your local device.\\n\\n2.\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0Type the command **traceroute <IP address of the destination host>**, and then press **Enter**. \\n**Note:** The output of the preceding command displays a list of hops that the packets are passing through on their way to the destination host. The RTT is also displayed.\\n\\n3.\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0Open the [AWS Management Console](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/signin/latest/userguide/console-sign-in-tutorials.html), and then identify the hop with the IP address of the Direct Connect endpoint.\\n\\n4.\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0Review the traceroute output, and identify any hops that have a higher RTT than expected. These hops might be contributing to the latency issue.\\n\\n5.\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0Check whether the hops with the latency issues are the Direct Connect endpoint.\\n\\n6.\u00a0 \u00a0 After identifying the hops that are causing latency issues, check for causes of congestion in the network configuration of each device in the patch.\\n\\n7.\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0\u00a0If the hop that's causing latency issues is the Direct Connect endpoint, then contact AWS Support\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-read-traceroutes\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How can I optimize file transfer performance over Direct Connect?\",\"context\":\"### Isolate and diagnose network and application performance issues\\n\\nYou can use utilities such as [iPerf3](https://iperf.fr/), [tcpdump](https://www.tcpdump.org/), and [Wireshark](https://www.wireshark.org/) to troubleshoot Direct Connect performance issues and analyze network results. Take note of the following settings that affect network throughput on a single TCP stream:\\n\\n* Receiver Window Size (RWS) - This indicates the maximum number of bytes the receiver can accept without overflowing buffers.\\n* The senders send buffers - This may limit the maximum number of bytes that the receiver can acknowledged. The sender can't discard unacknowledged bytes until it receives acknowledgment. Unacknowledged bytes may have to be retransmitted after a timeout period.\\n* The senders MSS (Maximum Segment Size) - The maximum number of bytes a TCP segment can have as a payload. The smaller the MSS, the less the network throughput.\\n* The Round Trip Time (RTT) - The higher the RTT is between the sender and receiver, the lower the available network bandwidth.\\n\\n**Tip:** It's a best practice for the sender to initiate several parallel connections to the receiver during file transfers. \\n \\n\\nFor more information, see [How can I troubleshoot Direct Connect network performance issues?](https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/troubleshoot-direct-connect)\\n\\n---\\n\\n Related information\\n--------------------\\n\\n[AWS Direct Connect features](https://aws.amazon.com/directconnect/features/?whats-new-cards.sort-by=item.additionalFields.postDateTime&whats-new-cards.sort-order=desc)\\n\\n[Best practices for configuring network interfaces](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/WindowsGuide/best-practices-for-configuring-network-interfaces.html)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-file-transfer\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"aws-media-services\",\"skill_description\":\"Designs, deploys, reviews, evaluates, audits, and troubleshoots video streaming workflows across AWS media services (MediaConnect, MediaLive, MediaConvert, MediaPackage v2, MediaTailor, CloudFront). Includes per-service validation rules, cross-service workflow patterns for live streaming, linear channels, VOD pipelines, and live-to-VOD, service-specific troubleshooting, best practices assessment, cost optimization, encoder settings, DRM, SCTE-35 ad insertion, epoch locking, and CDN cache configuration.\\n\\nServices: mediaconnect, medialive, mediaconvert, mediapackage, mediatailor, cloudfront\\nTasks: review, deploy, troubleshoot, audit, optimize\\nPersona: video-engineer, solutions-architect\\nWorkload: live-streaming, vod, linear-channel\",\"skill_name\":\"aws-media-services\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Search repost.aws knowledge center for MediaConnect SRT packet loss RTT troubleshooting", "parent_id": "f1545fee-14b0-4ca3-8bda-0234c2115b8d"}

{"id": "ea209a87-cada-4da4-8467-11c18cd5687c", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_haGLX1gOLBNMVTOCXNJ8YU", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/media/troubleshooting-srt-and-zixi-with-aws-elemental-mediaconnect/\",\"content\":\"Table of Contents:\\n- Troubleshooting SRT and Zixi with AWS Elemental MediaConnect (char 21-17732)\\n    - Contribution best practices (char 524-2134)\\n    - How the Zixi and SRT protocols work (char 2135-3507)\\n    - Provider sender recommendations (char 3508-5164)\\n    - MediaConnect receiver recommendations (char 5165-6787)\\n    - Monitoring and troubleshooting (char 6788-16966)\\n    - Conclusion (char 16967-17456)\\n    - **Further reading** (char 17457-17732)\\n\\n## AWS for M&E Blog\\n\\n# Troubleshooting SRT and Zixi with AWS Elemental MediaConnect\\n\\nSending video long distances can be challenging without a clear understanding of how your packets get from point A to point B. It also requires robust networking, sufficient bandwidth, and efficient encoding and delivery hardware. We will outline the best practices and troubleshooting techniques required to operate reliable transport using secure reliable transport (SRT) and Zixi with Amazon Web Services (AWS) Elemental MediaConnect.\\n\\n### Contribution best practices\\n\\nHigh availability contribution design requires redundancy. Two encoders output locked and egressing out different network circuits, carried over different providers, will provide both encoder and network diversity. These streams should be going to separate MediaConnect flows in separate Availability Zones (AZ). This basic architecture principle can achieve five 9\u2019s of availability.\\n\\nDiagram 1 shows a typical resilient and redundant streaming media workflow consisting of two encoders, two separate network providers (Direct Connect), two MediaConnect receivers, and a standard channel AWS Elemental MediaLive channel that runs in two AZs.\\n\\n[](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/fb644351560d8296fe6da332236b1f8d61b2828a/2025/02/11/SRT-and-Zixi-Contribution-Reliable-Transmission.png)\\n\\n*Diagram 1: A typical streaming media workflow.*\\n\\nIt\u2019s recommended to use AWS Direct Connect when possible. AWS Direct Connect provides a consistent network experience, with lower latencies and higher throughput rates compared to internet-based connections. If you have access to Direct Connect links you *must* enable VPC endpoints on your MediaConnect flows to confirm that no traffic egresses through Internet Gateways (IGW).\\n\\nIf you must send video through the public internet, just know your traffic is routed through multiple networks and service providers, increasing the latency and potential for packet loss. While Direct Connect and virtual private clouds (VPCs) are *more* reliable than the public internet, your feeds are not totally immune to issues in this configuration.\\n\\n### How the Zixi and SRT protocols work\\n\\nZixi and SRT have subtle differences in their technologies, which we will not get into here; however, they share many of the same approaches for delivery. SRT and Zixi are both built on user datagram protocol (UDP) and are both purpose-built for reliability and low-latency transmission over public networks. Both protocols also use automatic repeat requests (ARQ), which retransmits dropped packets. Also, both protocols allow you to set a latency value. This value adds delay in your stream, but also provides more time for dropped packets to be retransmitted and recovered. The larger this value is, the more delayed your video stream is, but also provides better recovery from dropped packets.\\n\\nDiagram 2 shows how packets are sent and received by the receiver and placed in a buffer for output. Packets lost in transit are \u201cdropped packets,\u201d which then the receiver sends a re-request for the packet. Packets re-transmitted and received in time are placed into the stream as a \u201crecovered\u201d packet. Packets that are not sent back in time, or lost again in transmission are \u201cnon-recovered\u201d packets.\\n\\n[](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/fb644351560d8296fe6da332236b1f8d61b2828a/2025/02/11/SRT-and-Zixi-Contribution-SRT-Block-Diagram.png)\\n\\n*Diagram 2: Packets sent and received by the receiver\u2014placed in a buffer for output.*\\n\\n### Provider sender recommendations\\n\\n**Latency settings should not be lower than 3x the peak round trip time (RTT) measured in MediaConnect.** If the latencies settings are too low, this may result in packets dropped. In Diagram 2, packet number seven is lost due to the network delay and low receive buffer settings. With a larger buffer latency, more time is provided to receive and place packets into the delivery output.\\n\\n**Latency settings should match the receiver application to achieve predictable results**. If a provider sends an SRT stream with a different latency value than the configured MediaConnect minimum latency, the higher of the two values will be used. For example, if the provider sends a stream with 500 ms latency, but the MediaConnect minimum latency is set to 6000 ms, the effective latency will be 6000 ms. Senders that expect acknowledgement responses (\u201cack\u201d) within their configured 500 ms latency, can timeout or pause sending packets. This behavior may vary by application.\\n\\n**The recommended send buffer for SRT is 25,000 packets**. If a sender has no buffer, packets are sent as soon as provided by the encoder, which can lead to inconsistent downstream timing. Increasing the buffer size may help address packet timing issues. The default SRT buffer size in some sender applications is 8,192 packets, which may not be adequate. If you see continuity or timing issues, increase this value to 25,000 packets, or more if needed.\\n\\nSRT applications typically contain additional settings that can be changed. You can read more about available settings and what they do. For most streams, default settings should be acceptable.\\n\\n### MediaConnect receiver recommendations\\n\\n**Do not set a primary source for failover *unless* the secondary is known to be lower in quality or reliability**. If the secondary is known to be less reliable (for example, the primary is on Direct Connect and the secondary is through the internet) then you should set a primary. Otherwise, do not set a primary source.\\n\\nUnless the source is properly configured for Merge, when a source fails over, the viewer will see content jump forward or backwards depending on the relative timing of each source. If no primary is selected, this jump will only happen once and stay on the second source. If a primary is selected in the configuration, the viewer may see two jumps, once during the initial failover, and again when the source returns back to the primary source as soon as the connection is re-established.\\n\\n**Set the Max Bitrate to 2x the expected bitrate**. The Max Bitrate needs an acceptable overhead established for a working buffer, for instances when packets arrive at the same time. By default, MediaConnect sets the Max Bitrate to 160 mb*.* For senders that send in excess of 80 mb the Max Bitrate setting needs to be set properly.\\n\\n**CIDR rules should *not* be set to 0.0.0.0/0**. In addition to the security implications, restricting CIDR rules to specific IPs (x.x.x.x/32) prevents accidental \u201cdouble publishing\u201d from misconfigured sources. Double publishing is when you send more than one stream to the same IP and port combination. This can lead to the wrong source showing in the output and incorrect metrics due to parsing multiple sets of incoming packets.\\n\\n### Monitoring and troubleshooting\\n\\nIf your stream is experiencing issues, there are several things you can do to determine the root cause. MediaConnect offers Amazon CloudWatch metrics that are used to measure the reliability of the stream. MediaConnect \u201cflow metrics\u201d only show the health of the active source. If you are using multiple sources for failover, MediaConnect also provides \u201csource metrics\u201d for individual source inputs. In addition to MediaConnect metrics, it is advisable to investigate the sending device for any relevant log entries or metrics during any interruption to your video stream.\\n\\nNext are six important metrics for monitoring the health of your flow. These will help you determine if an issue originates from the source and how to troubleshoot them.\\n\\n**#1 \u2013 Disconnects:** Source disconnects are typically caused by disruptions from the sender application or network path between the encoder and MediaConnect flow. For example, if an encoder is sending content to a MediaConnect flow as an SRT Caller that is rebooted, then a Disconnect metric with a value of one will be seen in the CloudWatch flow metrics.\\n\\nIf the network sending content is unstable or congested, leading to dropped packets, then the SRT or Zixi protocol will disconnect and a Disconnect will be registered in the flow metrics. This network level disruption is common in cases where the public internet is used to send the encoded video to MediaConnect.\\n\\nWhen an SRT or Zixi protocol disconnection occurs, the MediaConnect flow automatically attempts to re-establish the connection. The Connection Attempts metric shows how many of these reconnection attempts were made by the flow. When coupled with encoder logs, it can help provide additional insight into the cause of a disconnection. For example, a disconnect is logged on the flow, followed by two connection attempts but only one is received by the far-end encoder. It can be reasonably assumed that a network disruption prevented one of the connection attempts from being seen by the encoder.\\n\\nOther metrics such as Continuity Counter Errors, Jitter and Round-Trip Time can be used to understand if network connectivity is unstable enough to have contributed to these disconnections. MediaConnect only has visibility from when the source reaches the flow. If there are no logged issues at the sender, then engage with your ISP to determine if there are any network hops that may be faulty and introducing issues.\\n\\nMomentary disconnects will occur during scheduled maintenance. MediaConnect provides metrics to show when maintenance is scheduled and completes. Upcoming maintenances are listed on your AWS Health dashboard and notifications are sent to the email listed on the account.\\n\\n**#2 \u2013 Round-trip time (RTT):** This value represents the time it takes for a packet to be sent by an encoder and then acknowledged by the flow. You should verify that the MediaConnect latency settings is greater than three times the RTT. For example, if your flow\u2019s Max Latency value is 2000 ms, then you should confirm that the measured RTT metric is no more than 650 ms. If this metric is above, or spikes above, this recommended threshold the stream is at risk of d\",\"total_length\":17733,\"start_index\":0,\"end_index\":10000,\"truncated\":true,\"redirected_url\":null,\"error_code\":null}]}}"}]}], "label": "Fetch full AWS blog post on troubleshooting SRT/Zixi with MediaConnect for receiver flagging criteria", "parent_id": "f1545fee-14b0-4ca3-8bda-0234c2115b8d"}

**Note on sourcing:** The agent space's skill catalog provided to me does not include a MediaConnect/SRT-specific skill — a skill named `aws-media-services` surfaced in AWS documentation search results (it governs MediaConnect/MediaLive/etc.), but it is **not in my attached skill list and `skill_read` returned "Skill not found."** It's likely scoped to another agent role (e.g., the Chat Agent) rather than the Context Gatherer. All guidance below was instead sourced directly from AWS's official documentation and the AWS for M&E Blog ("Troubleshooting SRT and Zixi with AWS Elemental MediaConnect"), which is the canonical source for this exact rule.

### 1. MinLatency-to-RTT relationship (the rule)
> **"Latency settings should not be lower than 3x the peak round-trip time (RTT) measured in MediaConnect."**

- This applies to the **effective/recovery latency** of an SRT connection — SRT negotiates the larger of the sender's and receiver's minimum latency values as the actual recovery latency used.
- **Worked example from AWS:** If your flow's latency setting is **2,000 ms**, the measured RTT metric should be **no more than ~650 ms** (i.e., 2000 / 3 ≈ 667 ms). If RTT is at or above that threshold, the stream is at risk of dropped/non-recovered packets because there isn't enough buffer time for ARQ retransmission round trips to complete before playout.
- Rationale: SRT's ARQ (automatic repeat request) needs enough buffered time to detect a lost packet, request retransmission, and receive it back — that round trip consumes RTT, and you need margin (3x) to absorb RTT variability/jitter, not just the average.

### 2. Which receivers/flows should be flagged
A receiver (MediaConnect source/output) should be flagged as **at risk** when:
- **Measured/peak `RoundTripTime` metric exceeds ⅓ of the configured MinLatency** (i.e., latency ÷ RTT ratio drops below 3x) — this is the primary flagging condition.
- Watch for this condition occurring as a **spike**, not just sustained average — the blog specifically calls out "if this metric is above, **or spikes above**, this recommended threshold, the stream is at risk."
- Corroborating signals to confirm a flagged receiver is actually degraded (from MediaConnect's 6 key CloudWatch flow/source health metrics):
  - `SourceDisconnections` (unstable network/sender causing SRT/Zixi disconnects)
  - `ConnectionAttempts` (reconnection churn after disconnects)
  - `SourceNotRecoveredPackets` / `SourceDroppedPackets` / `SourcePacketLossPercent` (ARQ failing to recover packets in time — direct symptom of insufficient latency buffer vs. RTT)
  - `SourceContinuityCounter` errors (stream discontinuities)
  - `SourceJitter` (network jitter compounding the RTT margin problem)
- Additional mismatch to flag: if a **sender's configured latency differs from the receiver's MinLatency**, SRT uses the higher value — a sender expecting faster ACKs than the negotiated effective latency can time out/stall, which is itself a flaggable misconfiguration independent of RTT.

### Suggested deeper follow-ups
- If you want this applied concretely: I can pull `SourceRoundTripTime` and the current `MinLatency`/`MaxLatency` transport settings for specific MediaConnect flows/sources via `use_aws` (mediaconnect `describe_flow` + CloudWatch `get_metric_data`) and compute the actual latency:RTT ratio per receiver to flag violators.
- I could also retrieve the full `SourceNotRecoveredPackets`/`SourcePacketLossPercent` time series around a specific incident window to corroborate which flagged receiver actually experienced packet-loss impact."}]}], "label": "Search agent space skills/runbooks for MediaConnect SRT latency guidance."}

{"id": "56860898-8982-4b96-a0d2-4098253b3aa4", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Here's the rule, straight from AWS's MediaConnect SRT troubleshooting guidance:

**MinLatency vs. RTT**
- SRT's effective (negotiated) latency should be **at least 3x the peak round-trip time (RTT)** measured on the flow.
- Example: a flow with a 2,000 ms latency setting needs peak RTT to stay at or below roughly 650 ms (2000 ÷ 3). Go above that and you don't leave enough buffer for SRT's ARQ (automatic repeat request) to detect a lost packet, request retransmission, and get it back before playout.
- Note SRT negotiates the *larger* of the sender's and receiver's configured MinLatency as the actual recovery latency — so mismatched settings between sender and receiver matter too.

**Which receivers to flag**
Flag a receiver when:
- Its measured/peak RTT exceeds **⅓ of the configured MinLatency** (ratio drops below 3x) — including momentary spikes, not just sustained averages.
- A sender's configured latency differs from the receiver's MinLatency — the higher value wins in negotiation, which can cause a sender expecting faster ACKs to stall.

Corroborate a flagged receiver with these CloudWatch signals: `SourceNotRecoveredPackets`, `SourceDroppedPackets`, `SourcePacketLossPercent` (ARQ failing to keep up), `SourceJitter` (eating into your RTT margin), plus `SourceDisconnections`/`ConnectionAttempts` and `SourceContinuityCounter` errors as secondary indicators of instability.
